tagline: A thermostable hepatitis B surface antigen for a dissolvable microneedle patch - and a hard look at whether that is actually the right problem
summary: HePatch engineers the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for thermostability so it could be delivered in a dissolvable microneedle patch without a cold chain, benchmarked against the WHO controlled temperature chain condition of 28 days at 37 C. The dry lab scored 2,260 ESM2/Rosetta substitutions on a 238-residue E. coli construct, retained 989 after a ddG filter, and ranked candidates for the bench. What distinguishes the team is that it put the project in front of ethicists, legal scholars, Norway's national research ethics committees, a medical officer in Kenya's highest-prevalence county and a youth-led organisation in Nairobi's informal settlements - and then published the places where those people broke the project's own premise. Each stakeholder round is closed with a 'What changed?' box naming the previous assumption, the new approach and the updated framing.

dry.frameworks: A two-phase candidate-prioritisation pipeline for HBsAg substitutions. Phase 1 scores substitutions on sequence, structure and developability features; Phase 2 prepares checked ProteinMPNN and molecular-dynamics packages. Ethical reflection is structured on Kenneth Pimple's three questions for responsible conduct of research - is it true, is it fair, is it wise - with most of the human-practices work deliberately placed under 'is it wise'.
dry.dataviz: Original GIS cartography made by the team rather than borrowed from publications: population density, mean annual temperature, road network and hospital locations for Turkana and Nairobi counties, rendered in QGIS at WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), with every data source, resolution and limitation stated in the caption. Plus per-variant structural figures (WT, S54T, T56A, T113S) and the recurring 'What changed?' three-column comparison boxes.
dry.datascience: 2,260 ESM2/Rosetta-scored substitutions filtered to 989 by ddG; an earlier construct-v2 exploration ran AlphaFold2 and ProteinMPNN on six candidates, kept as a separately labelled history rather than merged. Provenance discipline is unusually strict: the pipeline records every input, output and source checksum, and the team states that the selected run reuses preserved ESM2 and Rosetta outputs whose original software versions and seeds were not recorded. Geospatial analysis used WorldPop 2020 constrained counts at 100 m, WorldClim 2.1 BIO1 at 30 arc-seconds, GADM 4.1 boundaries and OpenStreetMap amenity and road tags.
dry.software: A reproducible released pipeline containing the reusable code, tests and a synthetic example, with a separate archive preserving the selected run and its full provenance history. The model page carries a blanket disclaimer that none of the in silico output establishes expression yield, solubility, antigenicity, disulfide bonding, particle assembly or biological function.

good.publicEngagement: Education ran from kindergarten upward - children building model viruses and extracting DNA, sessions at Forskningstorget (the Norwegian public research fair), and presentations to biology students - with photo documentation of each. A separate Dialogues page records the conversations held with ethics and legal experts. The notable choice is a principle adopted from a stakeholder and applied to their own outreach: June Alfreds of Youth and Urbanism told them that raising awareness of a vaccine a family then cannot obtain does not build trust, it destroys it, and the team now treats that as a firm constraint on their own public communication.
good.ihp: UiOslo's IHP is the clearest example in this set of engagement that attacks the project rather than endorsing it, and every round ends in a published 'What changed?' box. Professor Kristin Bergtora Sandvik (Criminology and Sociology of Law, University of Oslo, fifteen years on the legal and ethical side of global health including vaccines and cold chains) pointed out that in Norway a vaccination appointment is also when a nurse weighs the child, checks for malnutrition, asks after the mother and notices when a family stops coming - so the team had been thinking about removing the syringe and the fridge without noticing they were also removing the healthcare visit. Professor Kristine Baeroe (Institute of Health and Society) refused to let reduced healthcare involvement count as an automatic benefit, and said of the recipients that children are 'the vulnerable among the vulnerable'. The design consequence is explicit: they moved away from designing for full self-administration towards a trained person being present, began investigating community health workers as administrators, and now describe HePatch as replacing a healthcare visit rather than an injection. Baeroe also told them that studying one country in depth beats a general claim about low-resource settings, which is why the project now writes about Kenya and specifically Turkana County; and she made the communication risk concrete by asking them to imagine a patch arriving in a community with no prior context for it, described as a cure, noting that mistrust in that situation is not irrational and that an intervention can be read as something done to a child rather than for them. Then the team did the thing most teams skip: they designed the Kenyan conversations as a falsification test, stating in advance that the alternative they were genuinely prepared to find - that cold-chain dependence was not a leading barrier in either setting - 'would have undercut the premise of the project as a whole'. Dr Vincent Ebenyo, medical officer at Lodwar County Referral Hospital in Turkana (16.8% hepatitis B prevalence in KENPHIA 2018, the highest county figure in Kenya), partly did undercut it: asked for the single biggest driver of low birth-dose coverage he named unsterilised shared cutting instruments used in ceremonies such as scarification and late health-seeking behaviour first, not the cold chain, which taught the team that transmission prevention and vaccine access are two different problems and a delivery-technology fix only addresses the second. He did confirm the core rationale with a precedent - his hospital had already switched from oxytocin to heat-stable carbetocin because local power instability made cold storage unreliable - but located the cold-chain failure specifically at sub-county and outreach facilities rather than the referral hospital, and noted mothers travelling up to 100 km who arrive a week or a month after birth, far outside the WHO 24-hour window. On self-administration he drew a comparison the team had not considered, that insulin-dependent patients are trusted to self-inject after training, while insisting that training must cover recognising side effects and knowing when to seek care, not just application; and he named the Pharmacy and Poisons Board as the body that would need to run sample trials, which is why the team now treats engagement with Kenyan regulators as part of the project path rather than an afterthought. Edwin Odhiambo, June Alfreds and nurse Steve Donell of Youth and Urbanism in Nairobi's informal settlements went further: Odhiambo said flatly that if HePatch can still only be administered inside a hospital, a mother gains nothing from the fact that it no longer needs a fridge, because she makes the same trip to the same limited set of facilities - a distribution and licensing problem, not a temperature one. Alfreds added barriers the team had not identified at all: teenage mothers unaware of the 24-hour window and stigmatised by providers, Social Health Authority registration requirements that undocumented mothers cannot meet, financial dependency and intimate partner violence determining whether a mother can attend at all, and a day queueing at a hospital being a day of lost income. Donell showed that stigma is locally specific rather than generic - in Nairobi hepatitis B is wrongly linked to sexual behaviour and drug use and mentally associated with HIV, whereas in Turkana the same disease is more often mistranslated as an alcohol-related liver condition - and recommended routing messaging through trusted community health volunteers and faith leaders rather than through specialists or the project itself. The result is a conditional value proposition rather than one universal pitch: transport and storage resilience in remote off-grid Turkana, and expanded distribution to non-hospital providers in Nairobi only if paired with a licensing pathway. The team also publishes two arguments against itself - that solving the cold chain for one vaccine could remove a reason to fund and maintain the shared cold-chain infrastructure every other vaccine depends on, and that since the WHO already permits some vaccines outside 2-8 C under controlled temperature chain rules, protein stability may not be the real bottleneck at all - and names its remaining gap honestly, that the Network for Adolescent and Youth of Africa could not attend, so the adolescent perspective 'remains a genuine gap in what we can currently report'.
good.realWorld: The need is framed at the level of a specific failure point rather than a continent: hepatitis B birth dose must be given within 24 hours, the conventional vaccine is an aqueous aluminium-adjuvant suspension that loses potency irreversibly if frozen as well as if overheated, and the cold chain in Turkana holds at the county referral hospital but not at the generator-dependent sub-county and outreach facilities below it, across a county of about 68,700 square kilometres served by eight hospital-level facilities spaced one to two hundred kilometres apart, with mean annual temperatures above 30 C across most of the inhabited lowlands. SDGs are used as tests, not labels: SDG 3 as primary with named targets 3.3, 3.8 and 3.b and a quantitative benchmark (28 days at 37 C, the WHO controlled temperature chain condition), SDG 9 and SDG 10 as supporting, and an explicit statement that these are intended contributions and not measured outcomes. They decline to claim a fourth, environmental SDG at all, writing that removing refrigeration and sharps could cut some material and energy demand but the polymer patch, sterile packaging and manufacturing have impacts, so a life-cycle assessment would be needed before any environmental claim - a refusal that is rarer and more credible than a claim. A trade-offs table pairs each possible benefit with its risk and with what would have to be measured to settle it (for example, delivery closer to home against work shifting to already stretched community health workers, measured by training time, workload, follow-up and user preference). The regulatory path runs through Kenya's own Pharmacy and Poisons Board rather than an external or parallel route. On equity they commit that a patch must not become a cheaper, less supported option offered only where health systems have fewer resources, and that any future use needs the same safety, dose and protection evidence as other vaccine formats - operationalised as comparing HePatch against the vaccination a child would otherwise receive rather than against no vaccination, because 'measuring our option against nothing makes it look better than it is'. What they claim now is bounded: antigen candidates designed and tested, no complete thermostable vaccine patch, no demonstrated lower emissions, lower cost or improved coverage.

gemsTakeaway: Design the stakeholder conversation as a falsification test, stating in advance which answer would undercut the project, then publish it when it partly does - and close every round with a three-column box naming the previous assumption, the new approach and the updated framing, so integration is auditable rather than asserted.
